title: I want, I like, I can
topic: רוֹצֶה, אוֹהֵב, יָכוֹל, צָרִיךְ + infinitive in לִ־
why: The verbs want, like, can and have to in the present, followed by an infinitive in לִ־: everything you need to say what you want, like, can or have to do. The infinitives of the unit's verbs are learned here as vocabulary, just before the review.

{"lessons": ["

Want, like, can, have to

These four verbs follow the present-tense rule: four forms, depending on gender and number. רוֹצֶה (to want), אוֹהֵב (to like, to love), יָכוֹל (can, to be able to), צָרִיךְ (to have to, to need to).

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
רוֹצֶה
rotse		רוֹצָה
rotsa		רוֹצִים
rotsim		רוֹצוֹת
rotsot
אוֹהֵב
ohev		אוֹהֶבֶת
ohevet		אוֹהֲבִים
ohavim		אוֹהֲבוֹת
ohavot
יָכוֹל
yakhol		יְכוֹלָה
yekhola		יְכוֹלִים
yekholim		יְכוֹלוֹת
yekholot
צָרִיךְ
tsarikh		צְרִיכָה
tsrikha		צְרִיכִים
tsrikhim		צְרִיכוֹת
tsrikhot

רוֹצֶה is conjugated like שׁוֹתֶה (final ה), and אוֹהֵב like כּוֹתֵב, with a small a in the plural: אוֹהֲבִים, ohavim.

יָכוֹל and צָרִיךְ have their own pattern: learn their four forms by heart. They have no everyday infinitive; in the exercises, you're given their root (י־כ־ל, צ־ר־ך).

", "

+ the infinitive in ל

As in English, these verbs are followed by an infinitive: \"I want to eat\" = אֲנִי רוֹצֶה לֶאֱכֹל. The Hebrew infinitive starts with ל, a bit like English \"to,\" and it never changes.

InfinitivePronunciationMeaning
לִכְתֹּבlikhtovto write
לִלְמֹדlilmodto learn, to study
לִקְרֹאlikroto read
לִשְׁתּוֹתlishtotto drink
לִישֹׁןlishonto sleep
לֶאֱכֹלle'ekholto eat
לַעֲבֹדla'avodto work
לָגוּרlagurto live
לָקוּםlakumto get up
לָבוֹאlavoto come
לָלֶכֶתlalekhetto go, to walk
לְדַבֵּרledaberto speak

The basic pattern: לִ + the root with o: לִכְתֹּב, לִלְמֹד. Before א or ע, the vowel changes: לֶאֱכֹל, לַעֲבֹד. The short verbs from lesson 2 take לָ: לָגוּר, לָבוֹא. Learn the others as they are.

", "

Saying what you like

הִיא אוֹהֶבֶת לִקְרֹא.She likes to read. [hi ohevet likro]
אֲנַחְנוּ צְרִיכִים לַעֲבֹד הַיּוֹם.We have to work today. [anakhnu tsrikhim la'avod ha-yom]
אַתָּה יָכוֹל לָבוֹא בָּעֶרֶב?Can you come this evening? (to a man) [ata yakhol lavo ba-erev?]
אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצָה לָקוּם!I don't want to get up! (a woman speaking) [ani lo rotsa lakum!]

אוֹהֵב and רוֹצֶה can also take a noun: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב קָפֶה (I like coffee), אֲנִי רוֹצָה תֵּה (I want tea). For a taste in general, Hebrew uses no article, just like English: \"I like coffee.\"

Only the first verb agrees: הֵן רוֹצוֹת לֶאֱכֹל, they (f.) want to eat. The infinitive stays the same for everyone, and לֹא goes before the first verb.
